prize_parts.citation: for developing the political-economy theory of trade policy, showing how lobbying and organised interests shape the structure of trade protection

statement.case_for: My preferred part and laureates are unchanged: B001, Grossman and Helpman. What changed is the citation. In round 1 I proposed to name both organised interests and the integration of innovation and growth into trade theory. After the exchange I narrow it to the political economy of trade protection, because three colleagues who share my first choice (Enflo, Fredriksson, Hassler) and one who does not (Krusell) argue the growth strand goes beyond the ballot's stated discovery. They also say it may overlap with the 2025 prize. I cannot verify that overlap from the evidence I have, so I would rather not make the award depend on it. The scientific case is that the protection-for-sale framework turned a long-standing qualitative claim, that organised interests bend policy, into a formal model with sharp cross-sector predictions. That made influence over policy a measurable object. From my own field's perspective this is the main reason it travelled beyond trade. Political scientists had long studied lobbying and pressure groups, but largely without an equilibrium account of what interest groups buy and what governments trade away. Attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: a long, tightly coupled two-person partnership with the central papers and the book, and no obvious uncredited co-originator at the same level. The core results are about thirty years old and have been tested, criticised and extended. The mixed empirical record is shared by almost every B001 supporter, so it is not what distinguishes B001 from its rivals. I weigh it as a real limit, and I do not count how many members prefer B001 as merit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is empirical. Tests of the protection-for-sale equilibrium are mixed and sensitive to specification, so part of the case rests on the framework's organising power and not on confirmed quantitative predictions. A prize for a framework whose headline predictions only partly survive testing invites the objection that it rewards an agenda. Narrowing the citation leaves out the growth-and-trade strand and so understates the pair's wider programme. My own assessment rests on general knowledge and on colleagues' statements, and I have not independently verified citation, impact or the prior-prize overlaps. Finally, a committee that prefers tested findings, or one that wants trade recognised through a different line, could reasonably favour B018 or the firm-heterogeneity candidate. B030's attribution gap would then have to be resolved.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson now proposes Autor, Dorn and Hanson for B018. She argues Dorn's role in the China-shock papers is substantive, and that Katz's skill-premium line is separate and should not fill the third slot. She treats the decade of replication and debate over shift-share designs as maturity.
responses.response: She persuades me on the name. My round-1 proposal of only Autor and Hanson was hard to defend on attribution, and Autor-Dorn-Hanson is a more stable core for a trade-shock citation than any set including Katz. That is why B018 stays my first alternative, and I would now propose the three-name set if the committee went there. I do not move it above B001 for two reasons. First, the task framework has antecedents outside the credited names, so the citation would have to be confined to the empirical evidence on labour demand and local labour markets. Second, the persistence and magnitude of the shock effects are still being re-estimated. I read that as a healthy sign, but it argues for waiting somewhat. This is a difference in weighting and not a dispute over quality, and I would not be reluctant to support B018 in a later year.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B002 first but now calls B001 a close alternative. He finds the mixed protection-for-sale record more worrying than B001 supporters do, thinks it makes the lasting value an organising theory, and says the B001 citation should not be widened to endogenous growth by implication.
responses.response: I agree on the citation and have changed it accordingly. On the empirics, I would say that an organising theory which made lobbying testable and produced three decades of structural and reduced-form work is the kind of contribution my own field also rewards. Political science has mixed tests of many of its central frameworks, and I do not treat that as disqualifying. Where I do take his point is that BLP has been validated through routine use in merger review and antitrust, while B001 has been validated mainly through research use. That is a real difference in kind, and I find the choice between them a judgement and not a scientific ranking. B002's credit set is the deciding issue for me. A three-name BLP core leaves out Bresnahan and Reiss, and Pakes's dynamic-games work sits partly outside it. B001 requires no such cut.

responses.point: Dreber keeps B030 first because the firm-heterogeneity framework has been confronted with micro data more densely than protection-for-sale. She treats the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum omission as the main weakness and says the two trade ballots are not scientific competitors.
responses.response: I agree the two ballots credit different achievements and should not be treated as additive. A configuration with both would also exceed the three-person limit. The density of empirical confrontation is a fair advantage for B030, and I weigh it. Two things still keep me from placing B030 ahead. The credited three leave out the people who established the exporter facts and parallel models. And as colleagues note, the pivotal contribution is essentially one 2003 paper, so the citation would be harder to word defensibly than a two-name one. If the committee can show that a Melitz-Helpman citation survives the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum gap, I would reconsider it. At present I do not see how to settle that within a three-name cap. I also do not see a Grossman-Helpman award as foreclosing later recognition of firm heterogeneity.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B001 first and records mixed empirical support as his main reservation. He says the case should rest on attribution, maturity and influence, and asks whether recognition in 2008 (trade) and 2025 (innovation-led growth) makes the committee less receptive to a trade-and-growth citation.
responses.response: That last question is the reason I narrowed the citation. A trade-and-growth citation invites the overlap objection, and I cannot verify the 2025 prize's coverage, so I do not want the case to depend on it. A political-economy citation avoids it, since the 2008 prize concerned trade patterns and scale economies, as colleagues describe it, and not why policy departs from efficiency. I also accept his point that his field, industrial organisation and trade, gives him a closer view than mine of the firm-level literature, and I have no basis to contradict his read on B030 attribution. I differ from him slightly in that I would not name the growth strand in the citation at all, since the ballot's stated discovery is the political economy of protection.

uncertainties: How much weight the mixed empirical record of protection-for-sale should carry against its conceptual and organising influence. I treat this as a judgement that colleagues weigh differently and not as a question evidence can settle.

Whether the narrowed citation is the right one, or whether the committee would find the growth-and-trade strand adds to the case without borrowing from recognition I cannot verify (the 2008 and 2025 prizes).

Whether the committee can settle a stable core for B018 (Autor, Dorn and Hanson) and confine the citation to the empirical evidence on labour demand. If it can, B018 would become a stronger rival to B001.

Whether a Melitz-Helpman citation for B030 could survive the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and how Helpman's credit on both trade ballots should be handled if a trade prize split the committee.
My assessments rest on general knowledge and on colleagues' stated facts. I have not independently verified citation or impact data, or claims about earlier prizes.
statement.conflict_note: No profile-based connection to Grossman or Helpman is apparent. My profile lists no collaboration or institutional tie with either, and they work in trade economics, not in my fields. For the alternative B036, I disclose that my profile lists a co-authored corruption paper with Torsten Persson and Bo Rothstein (Governance), and that Persson is at the Institute for International Economic Studies at Stockholm University, where I also hold my chair. I am therefore connected to a credited name on B036, and I would flag this as a possible recusal consideration if B036 were pursued. I disclose it without adjudicating it. Separately, I am a Stockholm University colleague, in a different department, of committee members Hassler, Krusell and Boppart, and none is credited on B001 or on my alternative B018. My own field (democratisation, measurement and quality of government) is close to B036's subject and to the political-economy side of B001, and I have tried to apply the same criteria as in other fields.
